statement: In healthy volunteers given ketamine into a vein in a laboratory, with salt water given to the same people as the comparison, scores on tests of learning and remembering words fall during the session and, in the two studies that tested again after the infusion had stopped, were no longer detectably lower within about an hour of its end; what happens to attention and to other thinking tests differs between laboratories and with the infusion used. In 15 volunteers given a 1-hour infusion, free recall of a 12-word list was lower on the ketamine day (drug F1,14 = 9.63, p = .008; drug x time F4,52 = 4.35, p = .004), most at 55 minutes (F1,13 = 18.79, p = .001) and still at 90 minutes (F1,13 = 6.25, p = .026), as was recognition of the same words (F1,13 = 17.48, p = .001; lower at 10 and 55 minutes) and, less markedly, a score for noticing repeated words as the list was read (drug x time F4,56 = 2.71, p = .05; lower at 55 minutes only); 13 of 15 people recalled less, 9 of 14 recognised less and 9 of 15 scored lower on the attention measure than their own pre-infusion level on the ketamine day, which is not a comparison with the salt-water day (Malhotra et al., 1996). In 15 men given three fixed infusions aimed at steady blood levels over 2 hours, measured and stable at 60 and 120 minutes in the two larger conditions while the smallest stayed below the assay threshold, recall of two spoken narratives fell with the condition (F3,41 = 5.11, p = 0.004), by 21.2 of the units the authors score, which they report as an 18.6% fall from the salt-water day to the largest condition, with immediate and delayed recall affected alike; no effect was detected on a colour-word task, a letter-watching task, word generation or a spatial memory task, which the authors themselves say may reflect how sensitive those tasks were (Newcomer et al., 1999). In a study of 18 volunteers given 40-minute infusions, with 14 to 16 of them behind each cognitive result, recall of a three-word set after a 10-minute delay fell at the larger amount (dose x time F8,120 = 3.4, P = .002) while immediate recall did not change (F8,120 = 0.0) on a task at which people recalled close to all three words on every day, so that comparison cannot show that immediate recall is spared; word generation fell (16.1 words after salt water, 15.1 and 12.9 at the two amounts; high against salt water F1 = 8.4, P = .007), vigilance changed by about one target of 30 (29.7, 29.6 and 28.5 correct; F2,26 = 8.6, P = .001), and a bedside test of global cognition did not change (F8,136 = 1.4, P = .2) (Krystal et al., 1994). The same study's card-sorting result (perseverative errors 6.5, 16.8 and 31.9) is a comparison of 6, 5 and 8 different people on their first test day with no baseline, not a within-person drug effect. Three things limit all of this: none of the studies reports a blinding check; the samples are 14 to 18 people, no study prints a confidence interval for a cognitive measure, and one of the three never tested anyone after the infusion had stopped; and the claim that the memory effect is separate from the attentional and psychosis-like effects rests on one adjustment at one time point and on six correlations in 14 to 15 people (from .02 to -.41), which are far too few to show that two things are unrelated. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In lab studies, healthy volunteers given ketamine into a vein remembered fewer words, and recognised fewer of them, than on a day when the same people were given salt water. The difference was largest while the drug was being infused. In the two studies that tested again after it stopped, scores matched the salt-water day within about an hour. Attention and other thinking tests were affected in one study but not in another, which the researchers put down to the different infusions and to how hard each task was. Everyone was tested once, in a laboratory, and the studies had 14 to 18 people each. Counts like 13 of 15 compare each person with their own score before the drug, not with their salt-water day.
population: Healthy adults screened to exclude psychiatric illness and, in one study, any previous use of ketamine or phencyclidine: 18, 15 and 15 people in three laboratory studies, with 14 to 16 contributing to several of the cognitive analyses
exposure: A single subanaesthetic amount of ketamine into a vein during the session (study conditions: 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes; a 0.12 mg/kg bolus then 0.65 mg/kg over 1 hour; three fixed infusions over 2 hours aimed at steady blood levels, of which only the two larger were above the assay threshold)
comparator: Salt water (saline) given to the same people on another day, with each day's own pre-infusion test as the reference
outcome: Scores on tests of learning, recall, recognition, attention, word generation, vigilance and global cognition during and shortly after the session
magnitude: Malhotra et al. (1996), n = 15 (14 for recognition): free recall drug F1,14 = 9.63 (p = .008), drug x time F4,52 = 4.35 (p = .004), lower at 55 minutes F1,13 = 18.79 (p = .001) and 90 minutes F1,13 = 6.25 (p = .026); recognition drug F1,13 = 17.48 (p = .001), drug x time F4,52 = 7.95, lower at 10 minutes F1,13 = 8.92 (p = .01) and 55 minutes F1,13 = 18.78; attention drug x time F4,56 = 2.71 (p = .05), lower at 55 minutes F1,14 = 8.79 (p = .01); 13 of 15, 9 of 14 and 9 of 15 people scored lower than their own pre-infusion level on the ketamine day. Newcomer et al. (1999), n = 15 men: total paragraph recall F3,41 = 5.11 (p = 0.004), immediate F3,41 = 3.92 (p = 0.02), delayed F3,41 = 5.03 (p = 0.005); fall of 21.2 units from placebo to the largest condition, reported as 18.6%; non-verbal recognition F3,40 = 2.93 (p = 0.045), described by the authors as preliminary; no effect detected on the Stroop, continuous performance, word generation or spatial delayed response tasks. Krystal et al. (1994), n = 14 to 18: 10-minute delayed three-word recall dose x time F8,120 = 3.4 (P = .002), immediate recall F8,120 = 0.0 at ceiling; word generation 16.1 (SEM 1.3), 15.1 (1.2) and 12.9 (1.3) words, dose F2,28 = 4.4 (P = .02); vigilance 29.7 (0.1), 29.6 (0.2) and 28.5 (0.4) of 30 targets, F2,26 = 8.6 (P = .001); MMSE dose x time F8,136 = 1.4 (P = .2).

evidence.locator: Methods > Procedure, Cognitive and Behavioral Measures, and Data Analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 302); Results, 1st paragraph (left column) continuing in the right column, and Figure 1 (p. 303)
evidence.extracted: Free recall of a 12-word categorical list was lower on the ketamine day than on the salt-water day in 15 healthy volunteers: drug F1,14 = 9.63 (p = .008), time F4,56 = 5.16 (p = .005), drug x time F4,52 = 4.35 (p = .004); lower at 55 minutes F1,13 = 18.79 (p = .001) and at 90 minutes F1,13 = 6.25 (p = .026). Recognition of the same words (n = 14) was lower too: drug F1,13 = 17.48 (p = .001), time F4,52 = 6.05, drug x time F4,52 = 7.95 (p < .001), lower at 10 minutes F1,13 = 8.92 (p = .01) and 55 minutes F1,13 = 18.78. The attention score fell less markedly: drug x time F4,56 = 2.71 (p = .05), lower at 55 minutes only, F1,14 = 8.79 (p = .01). Only for attention does the paper say what its individual count measures: 9 of 15 people fell from their own pre-infusion level at 55 minutes of the ketamine infusion, which is not a comparison with the salt-water day; the next sentence gives 13 of 15 for free recall and 9 of 14 for recognition without restating the time or the reference. All three measures come from the same word list, so they are not independent of each other.

evidence.locator: Results (continued), 3rd to 5th paragraphs of the left column; Figure 2
evidence.extracted: The memory effects at 55 minutes remained when the attention score from the same task was used as a covariate (free recall F1,12 = 6.55, printed as p = 0.25, which does not match the statistic and is almost certainly a slip for .025; recognition F1,13 = 7.05, p = .025). The ketamine-minus-placebo changes in memory were not significantly correlated with the changes in symptom ratings (free recall with BPRS total r = -.28, p = .31; with thought disorder r = -.31; recognition with BPRS total r = -.28, with thought disorder r = -.41, p = .14), while the two memory changes correlated with each other (r = .64, p = .01); with 14 to 15 people these null correlations cannot show that the memory and symptom effects are unrelated.

evidence.locator: Results > Cognitive Results > Paragraph Recall, only paragraph, and > Other Cognitive Tasks, only paragraph; Figure 4 and its legend (p. 112); Results > Cognitive Results > DMS (p. 112); Figure 5 and its legend (p. 113)
evidence.extracted: Recall of two recorded narratives fell with the infusion condition in 15 healthy men: total (immediate plus delayed) F3,41 = 5.11 (p = 0.004), immediate F3,41 = 3.92 (p = 0.02) and delayed F3,41 = 5.03 (p = 0.005), with a main effect of recall condition (F1,14 = 46.14) and no interaction between condition and recall condition, so immediate and delayed recall were affected alike. The mean fall in total correct recall from the salt-water condition to the largest one was 21.2 units, which the paper reports as an 18.6% fall. Non-verbal recognition also changed (F3,40 = 2.93, p = 0.045) but only in the univariate analysis and with post-hoc tests on 5 and 7 degrees of freedom, so the authors call it preliminary. No significant effect was detected, with adjusted or unadjusted p values, on the modified Stroop task, the continuous performance task, word generation or the spatial delayed response task, and no statistics are printed for those four.

evidence.locator: Results > Additional Clinical and Adverse Events, and Safety Measures, 1st paragraph; Results > Plasma Results, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Covarying drowsiness from the adverse-events checklist, and plasma cortisol, glucose, adrenaline and noradrenaline from the sample times closest to the tests, left the effect of the infusion condition on verbal and non-verbal memory unchanged, with no main effect of the covariate and no interaction, so the memory effect is not explained by sedation or by these blood measures. Steady blood ketamine levels were reached by 30 minutes in the two larger conditions, while the smallest stayed below the assay threshold (condition x time F9,125 = 73.62, p = 0.0001), and plasma norketamine never reached a steady level but rose throughout the infusion.

evidence.locator: Results > Memory (p. 206, right column, continuing on p. 207); Figure 4 (p. 207)
evidence.extracted: Word recall (n = 16) showed an interaction of amount, time and delay (F16,240 = 2.7, P = .0006). There was no interaction for immediate recall (F8,120 = 0.0), a non-significant trend for recall after a distracting task (F8,120 = 1.7, P = .1) and a significant interaction for recall after a 10-minute delay (F8,120 = 3.4, P = .002), with a fall at 0.5 mg/kg. Only three words were presented at each time point and immediate recall sat at or near three on every day, so the task could not show a fall there. On the 0.5 mg/kg day the fall in delayed recall did not correlate significantly with the rise in positive symptoms (r = .2), negative symptoms (r = .07) or dissociation (r = .2), in 16 people.

evidence.locator: Results > Mini-Mental State Examination, only paragraph (p. 205); Results > Measures of frontal lobe function > Vigilance (p. 205, continuing on p. 206) and > Verbal Fluency (p. 206); Figure 3, left panel
evidence.extracted: Global cognition on a bedside test (n = 18) did not change significantly (dose x time F8,136 = 1.4, P = .2; peak falls from baseline 0.7, SEM 0.4 after salt water, 0.2 at 0.1 mg/kg and 0.3 at 0.5 mg/kg; dose F2,34 = 1.6). Vigilance (n = 14) changed only at the larger amount and only slightly: 29.7 (SEM 0.1), 29.6 (0.2) and 28.5 (0.4) targets correctly identified of 30 (F2,26 = 8.6, P = .001), omission errors 0.3, 0.4 and 1.5, commission errors 0.1, 0.2 and 0.6 (F2,26 = 4.3, P = .03), reaction time unchanged (0.48, 0.46 and 0.51 seconds, F2,24 = 1.8, P = .2). Word generation in one minute (n = 15) fell: 16.1 (SEM 1.3), 15.1 (1.2) and 12.9 (1.3) words, dose F2,28 = 4.4 (P = .02), the larger amount against salt water F1 = 8.4 (P = .007); three people's tests were discarded because they were not finished before the infusion ended.

evidence.locator: Results > Measures of frontal lobe function > Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, only paragraph; Figure 3, right panel
evidence.extracted: On a card-sorting test, which cannot be repeated in the same person, the comparison is between people on their first test day only (salt water n = 6, 0.1 mg/kg n = 5, 0.5 mg/kg n = 8): perseverative errors 6.5 (SEM 0.8), 16.8 (7.9) and 31.9 (7.0), dose F2,16 = 4.6 (P = .03); trials to the first category 13.5, 14.6 and 35.1; total errors 12.8, 25.6 and 53.4 (F2,16 = 8.0, P = .004). The percentage of errors that were perseverative did not differ (54%, 62%, 58%), the number of correct items did not differ (70.8, 68.8, 65.6) and everyone completed all six categories. With three small unmatched groups and no baseline, this is not a within-person drug effect.

grade.reasoning: Within-person, placebo-controlled laboratory studies with randomized order start high (METHODS 6.3; round brief). Risk of bias -1: none of the three studies reports a blinding check and the condition is likely to have been recognizable; in one study the attention measure used as a covariate comes from the same word list as the memory scores, its degrees of freedom do not match the sample for several analyses and one printed p value contradicts its own statistic; in another the easiest tasks sat at ceiling and the card-sorting comparison is between unmatched groups; in the third the printed dose-to-dose p values are one-tailed and data missing at the largest condition are missing because of a drug effect. Imprecision -1: 14 to 18 people per study, with as few as 6 to 8 complete pairs behind the non-verbal memory result, and no confidence interval printed for any cognitive measure. Not downgraded for inconsistency: the fall in verbal learning and memory is found in all three laboratories, and the disagreement about attention, word generation and vigilance is explained by the different infusions and blood levels and by task sensitivity, which the authors of the steady-state study state themselves; a reading that treated that disagreement as unexplained would give very low. Not downgraded for indirectness, because the claim stays with healthy volunteers in a laboratory during the session. Independent replication: three laboratories (Yale and West Haven; the National Institute of Mental Health; Washington University) agree on the verbal memory finding, and the two later studies were designed partly to extend the first, so they are not blind to it.
